newsitem.title: UK: Flourishing fund industry to see more M&A activity.
newsitem.headline: Flourishing fund industry to see more M&A activity.

text.p: The global fund management industry is growing so rapidly that the current wave of mergers and acquisitions is expected to gather pace in 1997 as players strive to secure market share, industry sources said.
Among recent link-ups are Invesco and AIM; NatWest buying Gartmore; Dresdner capturing Kleinwort Benson and Hermes' joint venture with Liberty.
"The underlying dynamic is that fund management is a growth industry and the outlook over the next 10 years is very good," said a US fund manager in London.
"The two main forces behind it are the rapid globalisation of markets, and demographics -- the aging of the populations in most developed countries."
Martin Cross, a fund management analyst at UBS, agreed that the spate of fund managers buying each other, and big banks buying fund management groups would continue through 1997.

"Fund managers buying each other tend to be keenly priced but the latter are paying top dollar," he said. "They are looking for an alternative source of revenue, and for a relatively small outlay you get a big return from fund management." Smaller-scale M&A activity is happening nationally all the time but London, which has more global funds under management than New York, is in the thick of the international scrum.

UK houses want to elbow in on the US; US firms see the UK market only just starting to open up and the whole of Europe behind that. Germany has indicated that if it cannot be Europe's financial centre, it will build a commanding presence anyway.

Commerzbank is still hungry after devouring Jupiter Tyndall, Bankgeselleschaft lost Gartmore but is still looking. The UK's fiercely independent Mercury Asset Management, having shed SG Warburg, is seen by many as a tempting target.

Industry experts say fund management offers tremendous earnings growth and operational gearing. "It's also low marginal cost -- if you are managing 10 billion and you double it, you don't need to double the staff," said a UK marketing manager.

In contrast, traditional banking business is seen as capital intensive with bad debt cycles and expensive to set up and develop. Financial sector companies now want to balance revenues and load up with fees and commissions.
The principal entry barrier is that it usually takes a long time to develop a presence and a reputable performance record.
"If you set up in Tokyo now and hope to network it will take you an age," another fund manager said. "So you go out and buy a business with a recognised brand name."

UBS's Cross added that "rightly or wrongly, the perception is that investors want to deal with bigger fund managers from the point of view of safety." That may be prompting smaller groups to seek the protection of a bigger parent. Other managers say the current M&A spree also reflects the urgency to grab market share while its going. "The industry is developing very rapidly. But you have to be careful because it is still a people business. If your new team doesn't like the arrangement they just walk -- to your rivals," noted one.
From smaller centres, other asset management groups are showing ambition. The Netherlands has a powerful pension fund industry while South Africa's Old Mutual is spreading its wings.
Scotland has marketed its distance from the "crowd" in London so successfully that several Scottish houses -- Baillie Gifford is often named -- would be highly prized acquisitions.

"There is also Franklin Resources of the US, which bought Templeton in 1988 and set up in Edinburgh. It's going well and they might well want more in the UK," said a local fund manager. Another fund industry trend is to seek alliances which bring complementary skills. "It doesn't thrill a client to hear you just do fund management and he has to go somewhere else for custody. You must offer a package," said one compliance officer. The outlook is promising. But most managers see the industry dominated in a few years by a handful of global giants with a smaller second tier of big groups and the rest beneath, hoping to get acquired or relying on niche skills to be left alone.
